html:
An agreement of 313 between the Roman emperors Constantine and Licinius, who met at Milan, to tolerate all religions and in particular to stop persecuting Christians. Church property taken in the persecutions was to be given back.

It followed the Great Persecution begun under Diocletian in 303, the harshest the church had faced. The emperor Galerius had already ended it in 311 with an edict of toleration. The agreement at Milan confirmed this across the Roman Empire. It was less one formal edict than letters sent to provincial governors.

Constantine, who had fought under a Christian sign at the Milvian Bridge in 312, went on to favour the church. He gave it money and land, called the Council of Nicaea in 325, and founded Constantinople as a new capital. Christianity became the state religion in 380 under Theodosius I, with the Edict of Thessalonica.
sum: An agreement of 313 between the Roman emperors Constantine and Licinius, who met at Milan, to tolerate all religions and in particular to stop persecuting Christians. Church property taken in the persecutions was to be given back.
